obtained.how: the authors' draft manuscript ('Draft 4', Word file) posted openly on the University of Vermont's Vermont Monitoring Cooperative project page (project 1628, winter fish ecology); converted to text for searching (Blocketal_nd.html/.txt). The draft is public, not private

bibliography.checked_against: the draft's title page; Crossref for the published version
bibliography.corrections: complete the entry: Block, B. D., Stockwell, J. D. & Marsden, J. E. n.d. Contributions of winter foraging to the annual growth of thermally dissimilar fish species. Draft manuscript (Draft 4), Rubenstein Ecosystem Science Laboratory, University of Vermont; posted on the Vermont Monitoring Cooperative site. It was published as Block, B. D., Stockwell, J. D. & Marsden, J. E. 2020. Hydrobiologia 847(20): 4325–4341, doi:10.1007/s10750-020-04428-2 (Crossref). The published version is subscription-only and was not read: cite it only after checking the numbers below against it, or cite the draft explicitly as a draft
bibliography.note: The paper's in-text 'Block et al., draft manuscript' (§3.5.4, the winter paragraph in 03_synthesis_fish_to_forest.md, line ~240) is where this entry is used; show.mjs found no match because the key has no year.

claims.claim: in Lake Champlain's Keeler Bay 34 % of perch stomachs were empty in winter against 8–10 % in spring and summer
claims.location: Results, first paragraph (web-text p. 1; the draft has no page numbers)
claims.quote: winter (34%, n = 122), and low in spring (8%, n = 99)
claims.conditions: yellow perch, Keeler Bay (470 ha, 12 m max depth, ice 4–5 months), September 2018–October 2019; summer 10 % (n = 77); autumn 2018 39 % (n = 44); winter fish were angled with jigs and maggots, open-water fish taken in 2-h gill-net and fyke-net sets
claims.note: The authors warn that angling may have targeted actively feeding fish, so winter empty-stomach rates may be biased low.

claims.location: Results, section 'Bioenergetics model simulations'; Discussion (draft unpaginated; web-text p. 1)
claims.quote: winter foraging provides sufficient energy for overwinter growth in yellow perch
claims.conditions: modeled (FB4, age-3 fish, fitted to observed annual growth); growth rates positive in winter except lowest in February; condition rose through winter, but PTLC (lipid) was lowest in March
claims.note: Growth is the bioenergetics model's output, not a measured winter mass gain.

claims.claim: pumpkinseed ate rarely and lost lipid in winter
claims.location: Results, first paragraph and section on lipid; Discussion (draft unpaginated; web-text p. 1)
claims.quote: the sunfishes ate infrequently in winter
claims.conditions: 76 % of pumpkinseed empty in winter (n = 34); PTLC lowest in winter

claims.source_value: the draft contradicts itself: Results say pumpkinseed condition 'appeared to increase over the winter and summer and decrease in autumn'; the Discussion says PTLC and condition of both sunfishes were lowest in winter
claims.location: Results, section 'Percent total lipid content, condition, and gonadosomatic index'; Discussion (draft unpaginated; web-text p. 1)
claims.quote: In pumpkinseed, condition appeared to increase over the winter and summer
claims.conditions: Fulton's K from wet mass and total length
claims.note: Say 'lost lipid' (supported) and drop 'and condition' for pumpkinseed, or check the published version's Fig. 5.

claims.claim: modeled summer-peak consumption was 6.0 times February's in perch
claims.source_value: 6.0 times higher in summer than in winter (the text does not say February for perch)
claims.location: Results, section 'Bioenergetics model simulations', first paragraph; Fig. 6 (web-text p. 1)
claims.quote: daily consumption rates were 6.0 times higher and metabolic rates were 5.3 times higher
claims.conditions: FB4 yellow perch parameters, age-3 fish; modeled fish assumed at 4.0 °C in winter, otherwise min(ambient ~3.5-m temperature, 25 °C)
claims.note: Write 'summer against winter' for perch, or read Fig. 6 of the published version to confirm a February basis.

claims.location: Results, section 'Bioenergetics model simulations', second paragraph (web-text p. 1)
claims.quote: 10.6 times higher and metabolic rates were 5.7 times higher in August than in February
claims.conditions: pumpkinseed MODELED WITH THE FB4 BLUEGILL PARAMETERS (no pumpkinseed model exists); age-3 fish; August peak against February
claims.note: In a paragraph (§3.5.4) about how surrogate parameter sets diverge from field evidence, the rewrite should say that this pumpkinseed ratio itself comes from the bluegill surrogate. Bluegill: 17.8× (July against February).

tried.note: the published version (Hydrobiologia 2020): subscription ('Buy article'); not read

notes: The draft is public (UVM's Vermont Monitoring Cooperative), so it can be cited, but it is a pre-review draft whose numbers may have changed in the 2020 Hydrobiologia article; the human may want the published PDF through a library to confirm 34/8/10 %, 6.0× and 10.6×. Other values: winter diets were isopods and amphipods (perch, also fish) and isopods (sunfishes); average items per perch stomach 10.5 in winter against 528.4 in summer; pumpkinseed winter stomachs had the highest mean biomass (84.2 mg) though fewest items; perch gonads developed through winter, bluegill not until after ice-out. Caveat for §3.5.4's 'Yellow perch … roughly hold their lipid (Sullivan 1986)': in Keeler Bay perch lipid fell to its annual low in March.
